'''Walter Cooper'''  (born July 18, 1928, in [[Clairton, Pennsylvania]]) is an American scientist, humanitarian, activist, and educator. Primarily a research scientist, he was also heavily involved in civil rights work both in [[Rochester, New York]] and in [[Mali]].

==Education==
Cooper's parents, Alonzo and Luda Cooper, were strong proponents of education, and Cooper often said "Not to educate a child is the worst form of child abuse."<ref name="rochester.edu">{{cite web| url = http://www.rochester.edu/news/show.php?id=3250| title       = University of Rochester Honors Two Equal Rights Champions with The Frederick Douglass Medal| year = 2008| accessdate  = October 20, 2010}}</ref> He graduated from [[Clairton City School District|Clairton High School]] in 1946, where he was a star [[American football|football]] player; he was named All Monongahela Valley.<ref name=rochester />  His friend [[Dan Towler]], who had played high school football at nearby [[Donora, Pennsylvania]], convinced Cooper to join him at [[Washington & Jefferson College]].<ref name=rochester>{{cite web | last =Warren Hill | first =Lauren | title =Interview Subject: Walter Cooper | work =Rochester BLack Freedom Struggle Online Project | publisher =[[University of Rochester]] | date =May 21, 2008 | url =http://www.lib.rochester.edu/index.cfm?page=4495&Print=8 | accessdate = January 10, 2015}}</ref>  He earned a scholarship and played for the [[Washington & Jefferson Presidents football]] team.<ref name=jeff>{{cite web | title =Dr. Walter Cooper | publisher =[[Washington & Jefferson College]] | date = | url =http://www.washjeff.edu/dr-walter-cooper-1 | accessdate = January 10, 2015 }}</ref>
While there, he majored in chemistry and minored in physics and math, graduating in with a degree in Bachelor of Science from [[Washington and Jefferson College]] in 1950.<ref name=rochester /><ref name=washjefftrustees />

He originally attempted to enter industry, but he soon realized that the corporate world was demanding more of black professionals, and he decided to pursue a higher degree. He briefly attended [[Howard University]]. In 1956, he became the first African-American to earn a PhD in [[physical chemistry]] from the [[University of Rochester]]. Cooper often said "I became a scientist because I did not see any black scientists. I looked around and I saw black doctors, black lawyers, but no black scientists. I chose that as a challenge."<ref name="rochester.edu"/>

==Career==
Cooper was hired by [[Eastman Kodak]] as a research scientist in 1956. Starting out as a research chemist, he was promoted successively to senior research chemist, research associate and technical associate. In 1985, he was named manager of the office of technical communications, overseeing the publications and technical reports of 2,300 scientific and research personnel. In addition, he managed the Office of Research Innovation.<ref name=jeff />  During his career, Cooper published a wide array of scholarly papers in the fields of chemistry and physical chemistry and became the holder of three patents.<ref name=jeff /><ref>[http://www.geneseo.edu/news/nrap.php?pg=Commencement2005.html SUNY honorary degree citation]</ref> He retired from Eastman Kodak in 1986.

In 1988, he was appointed to the [[University of the State of New York|board of regents]] of the [[New York State]]. In 2003, he left the board and became a regent emeritus.

==Civil rights activities==
{{BLP sources section|date=February 2023}}

===Rochester, New York===
A man of the times, Cooper was heavily involved in community development and civil rights issues, especially educational opportunities and motivation. There was a great deal of social turmoil present in Rochester, as shown by the [[Rochester 1964 race riot|1964 Rochester Race Riots]]. Cooper served the [[National Association for the Advancement of Colored People]] (NAACP) as their Rochester branch president. He co-founded the Rochester branch of the [[Urban League]] in 1965, continuing to serve on the board of directors into the 1970s. He was also a board member of the Baden Street Settlement, a non-profit organization working with northeast Rochester residents to improve their quality of life.

When the [[Economic Opportunity Act of 1964]] was passed, Cooper took a leave of absence from Eastman Kodak to help form an anti-poverty  agency in Rochester called Action for a Better Community, Inc or ABC.<ref>{{cite news |author=Desmond Stone| title=What the Antipoverty Effort is All about | publisher=Times-Union | date=August 3, 1965 }}</ref> He served as the associate director for two years, then as executive director. The organization established a local version of the national [[Head Start Program]], along with other aid programs.

===Mali===
Cooper established Rochester's [[Sister City]] program with [[Bamako]], Mali in 1975. As part of the program he worked with [[Rochester Institute of Technology]] to establish scholarships for students from Bamako. Due to his work, he was named a Knight of the National Order of Mali<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.lib.rochester.edu/index.cfm?page=4710#box2 | title=Dr. Walter Cooper Papers: Box 2: Biographical: Folder 7  | accessdate=October 22, 2010}}</ref> in 1981.

==Family==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=February 2023}}
His wife, Helen, who was also a scientist and worked for Kodak prior to Cooper joining, died in January 2005. They had two adult sons.

==Recognition==
In 1975, Cooper was elected to the board of trustees of [[Washington & Jefferson College]].<ref name=washjefftrustees>{{cite web| url = http://www.washjeff.edu/content.aspx?section=1352&menu_id=378&crumb=649&id=90| title = Washington & Jefferson College: Board of Trustees| accessdate = October 22, 2010| archive-date = May 27, 2010| archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20100527190208/http://www.washjeff.edu/content.aspx?section=1352&menu_id=378&crumb=649&id=90| url-status = dead}}</ref>

In 2005, [[SUNY Geneseo]] granted Cooper an honorary Doctor of Humane Letters.<ref>{{cite web| url         = http://www.geneseo.edu/news/nrap.php?pg=Commencement2005.html| title       = WALTER COOPER, SUNY REGENT EMERITUS AND KODAK SCIENTIST, TO RECEIVE HONORARY DEGREE AT SUNY GENESEO'S COMMENCEMENT| year        = 2005| accessdate  = October 22, 2010}}</ref>

In 2008, Cooper received the Frederick Douglass Medal from the University of Rochester in recognition of his lifetime involvement in civil rights.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/democratandchronicle/access/1698135811.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&date=Sep+24,+2008&author=Bennett+J+Loudon&pub=Rochester+Democrat+and+Chronicle&edition=&startpage=B.1&desc=UR+institute+honors+two+with+Douglass+medals | archive-url=https://archive.today/20120717170849/http://pqasb.pqarchiver.com/democratandchronicle/access/1698135811.html?FMT=ABS&FMTS=ABS:FT&date=Sep+24,+2008&author=Bennett+J+Loudon&pub=Rochester+Democrat+and+Chronicle&edition=&startpage=B.1&desc=UR+institute+honors+two+with+Douglass+medals | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 17, 2012 | title=UR institute honors two with Douglass medals | publisher=Democrat and Chronicle | date=September 24, 2008 | accessdate=October 20, 2010}}</ref>

His papers are archived at the [[University of Rochester]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Cooper, Walter  | work =Books, Special Collections & Preservation | publisher =University of Rochester Libraries | date = | url =http://www.lib.rochester.edu/index.cfm?page=4710 | accessdate =January 10, 2015}}</ref>

In 2010, Rochester City School number 10 was named the Dr. Walter Cooper Academy School #10 in his honor.<ref>{{cite web| url         = http://www.schooltube.com/video/dc7a954b60aa493fb71d/Dr-Walter-Cooper-Academy-Naming-Ceremony-Part-1-Rochester-City-School-District
| title       = Dr. Walter Cooper Academy Naming Ceremony| year        = 2010| accessdate  = October 20, 2010}}</ref> The school emphasizes research and interactive learning, the methodology Cooper promoted during his time as a Regent of the State of New York and as the education committee chair of the Urban League of Rochester.

In 2020, Washington & Jefferson College renamed first-year dormitory Beau Hall to Cooper Hall in Cooper's honor.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2021-04-01|title=Introducing Cooper Hall|url=https://www.washjeff.edu/introducing-cooper-hall/|access-date=2022-02-25|website=Washington & Jefferson College|language=en-US}}</ref>
